title: Routing convergence histories for hybrid expert topologies
content:
Purpose
Quick capture of experiments and profiling traces showing how expert routing patterns evolve over long sessions (>=8k tokens) on hybrid expert topologies that combine capacity-limited experts and dense fallback. Goal: identify transient and steady-state behaviors that cause tail latency bursts and throughput variance, then propose mitigations we can prototype in the runtime.

Background / motivation
- Customers using long-context prompts (context window 8k-32k) with MoE variants report intermittent p50->p99 latency spread even at constant QPS.
- Hypothesis: routing decisions (gating) initially spread load broadly, then converge to a smaller set of experts during a session; convergence + per-expert capacity limits + KV cache priming leads to oscillatory backpressure and spiky device-level stalls.
- Target models in testing: Llama-3-MoE-30B-like (synthetic), Mistral-MoE-22B prototype, Qwen-MoE-34B-ish. We use synthetic prompts mimicking code+specs and long dialogue to stress repeated attention to same tokens.

Experiment summary (high level)
- Setup: Dedicated single-node multi-GPU pool (A100-80GB x8), same runtime build (kernel fusion + continuous batching), batch size target 64 tokens/request, KV cache enabled, prefix caching ON for repeated tokens, routing policy ungated fallback to dense when expert full.
- Workloads: (A) Rolling-dialogue (8k warmup then 4k streaming); (B) Document-edit (mass repeated entity mentions); (C) Randomized prompts (control).
- Metrics captured: per-expert enqueue depth, average switch rate (requests switching experts across timesteps), per-device stall time (ms/min), p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), KV cache hit rate, router decision entropy (bits).

Key observations
1) Convergence timeline: routing entropy decreases rapidly in first 400-800 tokens of a session for workloads A & B. For Llama-MoE it typically stabilizes by ~600 tokens; Mistral-MoE shows slower convergence (~900 tokens); Qwen-MoE variants converge fastest (~300 tokens) but to a smaller expert subset.
2) Expert hot-spotting: after convergence, 10-18% of experts receive ~65-80% of routed tokens depending on gating threshold. Hot experts exceed configured steady-state capacity and trigger synchronous fallback routing spikes.
3) KV cache correlation: as routing focuses on fewer experts, KV cache locality improves (per-expert cache hit rate +18–26%) but this is offset by queuing delays on hotspot devices.
4) Tail-latency windows: p99 spikes correlate tightly (Pearson r ~0.83) with per-device enqueue depth crossing threshold X (~512 queued tokens). Spikes are transient (30–90s) but significant (p99 up to 3.4x baseline).
5) Intermittent oscillations: system shows a ~45–120s oscillatory pattern where fallback to dense reduces per-expert pressure then routing re-converges, creating recurring p99 waves.
6) Scheduler interaction: kernel fusion + continuous batching hides some of the stalls until queue growth triggers backpressure at the GPU driver, causing hard stalls visible in nvprof traces.

Hypotheses derived from traces
- Early-session exploration by the gate helps accuracy but causes uneven warming of expert caches. When gate later converges, those warmed experts receive disproportionate traffic and become bottlenecks.
- Current fallback policy (on-capacity -> dense fallback) attempts to be correctness-preserving but creates synchronous bursts to dense paths which are not smooth — these bursts compete with normal dense traffic and increase tail latency.
- Batching heuristics that prioritize throughput (aggressive accumulation) exacerbate tail when expert hotspots appear; short-term latency SLOs are violated because the scheduler waits to form larger batches on overloaded devices.

Concrete mitigations to try (priority ordered)
1) Soft-load-shedding at gate: introduce probability-based diversion away from hottest experts once per-expert running queue > threshold. Keep probability small (5–15%) to preserve accuracy but reduce hot-spot intensity.
2) Staggered fallback: instead of immediate dense fallback for all overflowed requests, spread fallbacks over a short randomized window (50–200ms) to avoid synchronized spikes.
3) Warmup probing: during first N tokens of a session (configurable, default 512), bias the gate to sample a broader expert set to pre-warm caches more uniformly.
4) Adaptive batch cutoff: when per-device queue > Q_high, lower target batch accumulation time for that device to prioritize latency over throughput.
5) KV cache sharding experiment: shard per-expert KV caches across GPUs to reduce single-device memory pressure for heavy experts (complex, requires infra changes).

Preliminary micro-experiments (results)
- Soft-load-shedding (p=0.1) reduced p99 by ~28% on Llama-MoE workload A, p50 unaffected, throughput -3%.
- Staggered fallback (uniform jitter 100ms) reduced p99 variance across 5 runs and eliminated recurring oscillations in 4/5 trials; average p95 improved ~12%.
- Warmup probing (N=800 tokens) increased early-session throughput variance but reduced steady-state per-expert queue by ~22% after convergence; net p99 improvement ~15% across workloads.

Profiling artifacts (notes)
- nvprof traces: show device memcpy spikes aligned with sudden routing shifts (attached in linked_artifacts PR).
- Router logs: per-request decision latency negligible (~0.3ms), but gating distribution calculation correlated with increased mutex contention in the routing metadata store when many requests update per-expert counters concurrently. Suggest use of sharded counters or atomic estimators.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Accuracy impact: how do soft-shedding and probing affect downstream quality (perplexity / task metrics) for our canonical eval sets? Need automated eval with small prompt sets before enabling in production.
- Cost tradeoff: spreading traffic more evenly increases GPU utilization spread and possibly increases total GPU-hours for the same throughput — acceptable for some customers, not for committed Dedicated pools.
- Operational complexity: staggered fallback is simple to prototype; KV sharding is expensive. Which mitigations do we prioritize for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?

Next steps / action items
- (Ethan) Wire up small A/B pipeline to measure eval delta for soft-shedding on Llama-3-MoE-synthetic (Jenkins INF-2389 job). Target: 2k eval prompts across summarization/coding. Due: 2026-03-05.
- (Priya) Prototype staggered fallback in runtime branch + perf test harness. Run 10 stability runs. Due: 2026-02-28.
- (Hannah) Add router counter sharding spike-proof prototype; measure mutex contention. Due: 2026-03-12.
- (Marco) Collect customer workload analogs and map which pools prefer latency vs unit-cost. Due: 2026-03-08.

Notes to self
- Keep experiment traces in cloud storage under s3://redwood-prod/perf/moe/routing-conv/ and attach stable links before merging.
- Remember to check memory-walk traces (pagemap) for hot experts — saw unusual ATP readbacks once.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally
- runtime build: main@pr/1742, kernel-fusion=on, continuous-batching=enabled, batch-target=64
- models: use synthetic-MoE-variants from /mnt/models/synthetic (README describes gating seed)
- scripts: perf/run_moe_long_session.sh --tokens 12000 --workload rolling-dialogue --capture nvprof
- expected artifacts: nvprof.csv, router_decisions.log, per_expert_queues.json (small), p99_summary.csv

Unresolved: need to validate whether Qwen-MoE specific gate function parameters are causing faster convergence; initial signs point at higher gate weight sparsity. Tick INF-2402 to follow up.

End of notes
